chunks: Muhammad al-Halabi asked him about the oil of henna and the oil of violet, asking: 'Do we anoint ourselves with it when we intend to enter the state of Ihram?' He said:

He said: 'Yes, and it does not contradict the earlier narrations, because the prohibition in the earlier narrations was directed only towards oils that contain perfume, such as musk and ambergris. There is no prohibition on the oil of violet and what resembles it, even if it is perfumed, and there is no contradiction between them in any case. It is permissible that the permissibility of using the oil of violet applies only when its scent disappears at the time of contracting the Ihram, or that this is specific to the state of necessity and need for its use, where one finds no alternative. It is also permissible that the oil of violet is among those whose scent has already faded, because if it is so, it follows the ruling of the Shiraj (a type of oil), which indicates this.'

key_terms.الشِّيرَاجِ: Shiraj, a type of oil used as a reference for permissible scented oil
key_terms.الْإِحْرَام: The state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: Can I use scented oil or henna when entering Ihram for Hajj?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration to resolve the apparent contradiction between general prohibitions on scented oils and the permissibility of specific substances like violet oil. The Imam explains that the restriction targets strong, lasting perfumes such as musk and ambergris, whereas lighter scents like violet are permitted because their fragrance dissipates or is distinct enough not to violate the spirit of the Ihram restrictions. This highlights the Shia scholarly method of reconciling narrations by distinguishing between the essence of the prohibition and the specific characteristics of the substances involved.
